newsitem.title: USA: Dollar edges up on stocks, German rate hike doubts.
newsitem.headline: Dollar edges up on stocks, German rate hike doubts.

text.p: The dollar rose against the Japanese yen and the mark Monday, buoyed by an impressive recovery on Wall Street and remarks from a member of Germany's central bank which cast doubt on prospects for higher German interest rates.

After tumbling 247 points to end at 7,695 Friday -- the second largest single-day point loss on record -- the Dow Jones industrial average battled back from early losses Monday to end up 109 points at 7,803.
The dollar, which had fallen in tandem with stocks for much of last week, rose as the blue chip index turned positive and charged higher in afternoon trading.
"We really traded in lock-step with the Dow for much of the day," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long Term Credit Bank of Japan.
The dollar edged up to 1.8340 marks from 1.8190 Friday. It also rose to 118.00 yen from 117.42.

Supporting the dollar against the yen was a report from the Japanese Ministry of Finance showing that Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus climbed 70 percent in July to 849 billion yen -- far less than the 100 percent rise that some analysts had feared.

Worries that a burgeoning Japanese surplus might fuel trade tensions with the United States and calls for a more competitive, lower dollar have boosted the yen at the expense of the U.S. currency of late. Dealers said Monday's figures soothed these fears somewhat.

Also helping the dollar were remarks from Hans-Juergen Krupp, a member of the Bundesbank's policy-setting committee, who said Monday that a rise in German interest rates at the present time would be "very damaging" to the German economy.
Krupp added that recent mark weakness was worrisome but said he saw little evidence that the weaker currency was fueling inflation.

Traders had feared the Bundesbank might nudge interest rates higher this week in order to curb the mark's fall and ward off inflation pressures, but Krupp's comments suggested such a move was unlikely.

"The comments highlight the fact that Germany's economy is not running away and that they are not importing inflation, so there is no real reason to hike rates," said Robert Sabia, vice president at ING Barings Capital Markets.
Dealers said dollar activity was kept in check Monday by caution ahead of a meeting of the Federal Reserve's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) Tuesday.
Like the Bundesbank, which will meet Thursday, the Fed is not expected to change interest rates at its regularly scheduled gathering.
In other trade Monday, the dollar rose to 1.5170 Swiss francs from 1.5035 Friday, and slipped to Canadian $1.3883 from C$1.3908.
The British pound slipped to $1.6060 from $1.6095 on Friday.
